title: Pulmonary Tuberculosis Complicated by Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura: A Case Report and Literature Review
case_text:
On April 2, 2023, a 53-year-old man presented to our hospital with weight loss and intermittent cough and fever for 11 months and dizziness and weakness for 3 days. His medical history included gout for 14 years and hypertension for 5 years. Eleven months before presentation, the patient visited a local clinic for weight loss, cough, and fever (Figure 1). Chest computed tomography (CT) revealed pulmonary infiltration. The skin tuberculin purified protein derivative test was positive. He was diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis. Anti-tuberculosis treatment was started with isoniazid, rifampicin, and moxifloxacin. Three days before admission to our hospital, the patient reported dizziness and weakness, and he was transferred to our hospital.
Upon admission to our hospital, the patient was awake but slightly lethargic. His vital signs were as follows: temperature, 37.4 C; pulse, 91 beats/min; respiration, 20 breaths/min; blood pressure, 143/94 mmHg; and oxygen saturation, 93% on room air. The results of the physical examination were unremarkable, excluding lip cyanosis, decreased breath sounds in the right lower chest, and several tophi in the feet and hands. There was no skin rash. Electrocardiography revealed sinus rhythm with biphasic T waves in the lateral leads. Chest X-ray revealed multiple bilateral patchy infiltration with increased interstitial markings (Figure 2). The laboratory tests included a white blood cell count of 4.5 x 109/L, neutrophil percentage of 64.8%, lymphocyte percentage of 13.0%, red blood cell count of 2.2 x 1012/L, hemoglobin level of 65 g/L, platelet count of 15.0 x 109/L, creatinine level of 345.4 micromol/L (normal range, 60.0-120.0 micromol/L), and troponin I level of 2.3 microg/L (normal, <0.1 microg/L). We made a diagnosis of secondary tuberculosis, acute renal insufficiency, and thrombocytopenia.
After hospital admission, anti-tuberculosis treatment with isoniazid, rifampicin, and moxifloxacin was continued. Amlodipine was given for hypertension, atorvastatin was given for acute coronary syndrome, and dexamethasone (10 mg, intravenous) was given because of thrombocytopenia (PLASMIC score = 5). One day after hospital admission, the patient developed fever with a temperature of 37.8 C. The laboratory tests revealed a procalcitonin level of 0.5 ng/mL. Anti-bacterial treatment with piperacillin-tazobactam was initiated. On April 4, 2023, the patient had a generalized seizure lasting for 3 min. Head CT revealed a small intracranial hemorrhage in the right occipital lobe. Valproate, levetiracetam, and midazolam were given. Blood tests revealed that the creatinine level had increased to 437.0 micromol/L and the platelet count had decreased to 10.1 x 109/L. His daily urine output was also reduced to 300 mL. Furosemide was given for diuresis. Recombinant thrombopoietin and platelet transfusion were given to correct thrombocytopenia. The patient was transferred into the intensive care unit (ICU) for close monitoring.
Four days after transfer to the ICU (April 8, 2023), the patient gradually became comatose. The repeated laboratory tests revealed metabolic acidosis, a platelet count of 30.3 x 109/L, and a creatinine level of 405.9 micromol/L. He received endotracheal intubation, and he was maintained on mechanical ventilation. Continuous renal replacement therapy was also initiated. One week after ICU admission, bone marrow biopsy was performed, which revealed active myeloproliferation with 65% nucleated myeloid cells, active granulopoiesis with predominantly neutrophil granulocytes and metamyelocytes, active erythropoiesis with polychromatic and orthochromatic normoblasts, and a normal karyotype. The blood smear revealed schistocyte and reticulocyte percentages of <1% and 10.5%, respectively. In addition, blood ADAMTS13 activity was 1.8% (normal range, 42.1%-126.3%), and the anti-ADAMTS13 antibody test was positive. Considering the patient's medical history and laboratory test results, we made a diagnosis of TTP. After two sessions of plasma exchange treatment (2000 mL each time, April 13 and 15), the patient's mental status returned to normal. He was extubated on April 16, 2023 and transferred to the medical floor on April 21, 2023. Brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed small infarcts in the bilateral parietotemporal lobes. A repeated examination revealed a gradually increased platelet count of 167.2 x 109/L and a decreased creatinine level of 320.2 micromol/L. Chest X-ray revealed no pulmonary infiltration. The patient was discharged from the hospital on April 27, 2023. During the clinic visit 1 month later, the patient reported no clinical symptoms, and his platelet count and creatinine level were 140.4 x 109/L and 315.3 micromol/L, respectively. His anti-tuberculosis treatment lasted for 10 months, and sputum acid-fast bacillus staining was negative.

You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Tuberculosis
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: pulmonary tuberculosis complicated by thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
